lectures.title: Complexity vs Flexibility: The systemd Controversy

cues.en: In this lecture.
I want to talk a little bit about the debate about System D, just to make it clear, I do do not want
to be part of that debate, but I still feel like I should present you some points with that one.
So especially once it when it became introduced to more and more Linux distributions like Ubuntu, it
was rather polarizing in the Linux community.
Critics said it's like overly complex.
They say it's suffering from feature creep.
We don't need it.
The architecture violates the Unix philosophy, which is that each program should do one thing well
and programs should work together.
And for example, that we should use standard input and output to allow combining.
And those tools should not be overly complex.
It can only run on Linux system and the concept it introduced compared to the init system on Linux or
most Linux distributions we're using before is that a lot of things were being done in parallel and
this can be detrimental of performance in certain scenarios.
So for example, if we would boot from especially for example, a DVD, if we do a lot of things in
parallel, the drive might be just spinning around, trying to handle everything in parallel.
And on those really, for example, on a DVD, it might be faster not to parallel paralyze the boot
process, but to do one thing after another because then the drive might be able to read the data more
efficient.
So there were quite a few points against introducing systemd to the Linux distributions.
Also, some people did not seem to like the maintainer of systemd, but that also seems to be another
discussion.
But um, systemd has enormous advantages.
A system nowadays has to be highly dynamic and the configuration might change on runtime.
We might just plug in an ethernet cable to our system and then we unplug it and we wanted to connect
to Wi-Fi and then maybe we want to have some services started or shut down depending on what kind of
network we are in.
So a system nowadays can be highly dynamic and we need an extensive way to set it up and to configure
it to adapt to all of those changes.
Um, we might also that's actually something that we can do with systemd.
We can have a server like a server process, a server service that only launches if we access a certain
port on our machine.
So we could have a web server that's not even running in the background and only when the first requests
hits that server, then it's actually launching that.
And systemd allows us to configure something like this.
Um, the next thing is that the system boot process, you will see that later here in this chapter it
tries to paralyze the boot process and this makes sense on somewhat modern drives.
So even on slow SSDs, this is way faster than using the previous init system where one thing would
be done after the other.
In addition, systemd offers many unique features.
So for example, we can have a service and it's a little bit of setup, but we could for example have
a service that we could be able to upgrade at a later date and no connections are being lost.
Everything still works.
Or we can have a backup script that only works if a certain amount is present and we can really specify
those dependencies on a really deep level.
And this is something that only systemd can offer us.
So I personally I do see the big advantages of systemd.
I see the point that it's a little bit more complex and that we do have quite a few configuration files,
but we do get advantages that we might want to have in a modern system.
Um, anyway, no matter how you stand for this discussion, uh, systemd is currently used by many Linux
distributions and thus we should learn it and we should become familiar with it so that we can use it.
So this is a little bit the controversy about systemd or the debate that has happened, but I feel like
it has mostly been decided for most distributions in favor of systemd.
So with that in mind, let's now start to have a look at systemd and let's now have a look at the general
structure of systemd, but that's the topic of the next lecture.
